legend: There is a permutation†$$$^\dagger$$$ p$$$p$$$ of size n$$$n$$$ that you are trying to sort. To do so, you may perform up to 20$$$20$$$ operations of the following form:

Select a subset of distinct indices i1,i2,⋯ik$$$i_1, i_2, \cdots i_k$$$ such that the value of pi1⊕pi2⊕⋯⊕pik$$$p_{i_1} \oplus p_{i_2} \oplus \cdots \oplus p_{i_k}$$$, where ⊕$$$\oplus$$$ represents the bitwise XOR operation, is zero.
Sort the values of p$$$p$$$ on indices i1,i2,⋯ik$$$i_1, i_2, \cdots i_k$$$.

For example, for p=[7,3,4,1,2,6,5]$$$p = [7, 3, 4, 1, 2, 6, 5]$$$, you could choose the indices [2,4,5]$$$[2, 4, 5]$$$, since p2⊕p4⊕p5=1⊕2⊕3=0$$$p_2 \oplus p_4 \oplus p_5 = 1 \oplus 2 \oplus 3 = 0$$$. After this operation, p$$$p$$$ would be equal to [7,1,4,2,3,6,5]$$$[7, 1, 4, 2, 3, 6, 5]$$$.
It can be shown that if it is possible to sort the permutation in any number of operations, then it is possible in at most 20$$$20$$$.

†$$$^\dagger$$$ A permutation of length n$$$n$$$ is an array consisting of n$$$n$$$ distinct integers from 1$$$1$$$ to n$$$n$$$ in arbitrary order. For example, [2,3,1,5,4]$$$[2, 3, 1, 5, 4]$$$ is a permutation, but [1,2,2]$$$[1, 2, 2]$$$ is not a permutation (2$$$2$$$ appears twice in the array), and [1,3,4]$$$[1, 3, 4]$$$ is also not a permutation (n=3$$$n=3$$$ but there is 4$$$4$$$ in the array).

The first line of each test case contains a single integer n$$$n$$$ (1≤n≤2⋅105$$$1\le n \le 2\cdot 10^5$$$) — the size of the permutation.
The second line of each test case will contain n$$$n$$$ distinct integers p1,p2,⋯pn$$$p_1, p_2, \cdots p_n$$$ (1≤pi≤n$$$1 \le p_i \le n$$$) — the elements of p$$$p$$$.
